supplement.where: Appendix 1: AI augmented ideation tool, PDF pp. 28-29 (printed pp. xxvi-xxvii). No separate external statistical supplement is referenced.
supplement.holds: Screenshots of the tool overview, persona generation, persona contributions and task-solution input. The included appendix contains no additional statistical tables, SDs or SEs.

paper_design_summary: University of Regensburg students were randomly assigned to a custom GPT-4 Turbo ideation tool or no AI and then worked in teams on an elderly-healthcare innovation and an automotive business-model innovation (PDF pp. 4 and 12-14, Introduction and Methodology). The paper reports 70 students in 24 teams producing 48 ideas; blinded experts scored idea quality and classified innovation types (PDF pp. 12-15, sections 4-4.2). The study used separate rooms and team stations in a supervised student session, coded lab_rct under the codebook, although the authors call it a framed/controlled field experiment (PDF pp. 1 and 12-14).

studies.label: Team ideation experiment: elderly healthcare and automotive business models

assignment.what_was_assigned: Participants were assigned to the experimental group with access to the GenAI-augmented tool or the control group without AI, then organized into teams. Both arms completed the same two tasks. The randomization procedure and allocation ratio are not given.
assignment.quote: In the first phase, participants are randomly assigned to either an experimental group or a control group.
assignment.locator: PDF p. 12 (printed p. 10), section 4 Methodology; also PDF p. 4 (printed p. 2), Introduction

arms.name: GenAI-augmented ideation tool
arms.description: Student teams brainstormed with a custom GPT-4 Turbo tool offering dynamically generated expert personas, then submitted agreed solutions; AI access continued during idea production (PDF pp. 4 and 12-14).

arms.name: Traditional team ideation without AI
arms.description: Student teams received identical tasks and background information, brainstormed without AI, and submitted solutions using Google Forms (PDF pp. 12-15, sections 4-4.2).

participants.exclusions: No exclusions, attrition counts or participant-flow breakdown are reported. The paper says the study involved 70 students in 24 teams generating 48 ideas; 70 is entered as the reported study sample contributing the analyzed outputs, not an explicitly enumerated assignment-stage count. Arm counts are not stated. The general description of three-person teams is not fully reconciled with the total headcount (PDF pp. 12-15).
participants.who: Business, economics and information systems students at the University of Regensburg, with coursework in International Management and Strategic Management (PDF pp. 13-14, printed pp. 11-12, section 4.1).
participants.quote: The study involved 70 students in 24 teams, generating 48 unique ideas.
participants.locator: PDF p. 14 (printed p. 12), section 4.1 Research design and approach; PDF p. 15 (printed p. 13), analysis of mean scores per idea and combined tasks

ai_tool.name_model: Custom GenAI-augmented ideation tool using OpenAI GPT-4 Turbo (PDF p. 4, printed p. 2; section 4.1 calls the backend GPT-4).
ai_tool.how_used: Teams used a chat-like interface to discuss problems with four generated expert personas. They could refine the problem and regenerate personas; personas offered ideas and feedback, and automated prompt sequencing supplied the conversation history. The paper states temperature zero. The tool logged interactions and saved a task solution once team consensus was reached (PDF p. 13, printed p. 11, section 4.1; Appendix 1, PDF pp. 28-29).

task.description: Each team developed one concrete solution for a product/service innovation in elderly healthcare and one for a business-model innovation in the automotive industry considering autonomous driving. Both tasks were completed under the assigned AI/no-AI condition (PDF p. 12, printed p. 10, section 4).
task.duration: 45-minute maximum task duration, with earlier submission allowed (PDF p. 14, printed p. 12, section 4.1).

outcomes.name: Aggregated idea-quality score
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Aggregate of the Dean et al. idea-quality evaluation criteria. The paper groups these criteria as novelty, feasibility, relevance and specificity (PDF p. 23, printed p. 21, Discussion). This is the overall output-quality measure, listed first under the codebook preference; the paper does not explicitly designate a primary outcome. An expert panel rated submitted team solutions on a 7-point Likert scale; evaluators were blinded to group assignment (PDF p. 4, printed p. 2, Introduction; PDF p. 12, printed p. 10, Methodology; PDF p. 15, printed p. 13, section 4.2). The analysis compares mean quality scores per idea and combines both tasks (PDF p. 15, sections 4.2 and 5); the 48 generated ideas are the output units, not 48 people (PDF p. 14, printed p. 12, section 4.1). No participant- or team-clustered precision is reported. Robustness variants are kept in this outcome: independent t-test and regression (PDF p. 18, Tables 2 and 3), bootstrap distributions of p-values with 1000 resampled iterations (PDF pp. 19-20, Figure 4 and text), and Cohen's d bars without numeric labels (PDF p. 20, Figure 5). No exact d was inferred from bar height.

contrasts.reported: Experimental mean = 4.583; control mean = 3.546. Table 2: t = -4.450938; p = 0.000056. Table 3: coefficient = 1.037037; p = 0.000054; R-squared = 0.301027. The Table 3 numeric column is headed t-test, but the accompanying text identifies these values as regression coefficients. Arm SDs, arm sample counts, SEs and confidence intervals are not printed; Cohen's d is shown only as an unlabeled bar in Figure 5.

outcomes.name: Innovation category (Task 1: regular, revolutionary, niche, architectural)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Expert assessment categorized ideas using the Abernathy and Clark innovation matrix (PDF pp. 12 and 15, printed pp. 10 and 13, sections 4 and 4.2). The reported analysis uses only Task 1 because Task 2 already specified an autonomous-driving problem (PDF p. 17, printed p. 15, Results). Point-biserial correlations with the category indicators are reported together as one categorical output outcome. This classifies individual ideas; it is not a measure of similarity or diversity across different teams. The PDF does not give a separate analysis count for Task 1, so n_units is null rather than inferred from the total team count. Hypothesis H5 concerns the likelihood of revolutionary ideas (PDF p. 11, printed p. 9, Table 1).

contrasts.reported: Point-biserial correlations: regular innovations r = 0.209, p = 0.328; revolutionary innovations r = 0.275, p = 0.193; niche innovations r = -0.251, p = 0.237; architectural innovations r = -0.103, p = 0.633. The paper states that none is statistically significant (p > 0.05). No category counts, percentages or confidence intervals are printed.

eligibility.reason: Random assignment to access versus no access to generative AI is explicit (PDF p. 12, printed p. 10, section 4). The reported study sample is 70 students, not the 48 ideas or 24 teams (PDF p. 14, printed p. 12, section 4.1); the PDF supplies no separate post-exclusion flow or arm headcounts. Blinded experts evaluated the teams' creative outputs on a 7-point idea-quality scale (PDF p. 4, Introduction; PDF pp. 12 and 15, sections 4 and 4.2). Thus all three screening criteria are met on the reported sample. The output-level analysis and missing cluster-aware precision remain extraction limitations, not screening exclusions.

one_line_finding: AI-assisted teams received higher aggregate idea-quality ratings than control teams (means 4.583 versus 3.546; t = -4.450938, p = 0.000056; PDF p. 16, printed p. 14, Results, and PDF p. 18, printed p. 16, Table 2).
open_questions: PDF p. 14 gives a total of 70 students but no arm headcounts or allocation/exclusion flow. Confirm the analyzed headcounts by arm and reconcile the described three-person teams with 24 teams (PDF pp. 12-14).

Was the session part of ordinary coursework? The authors call it a framed/controlled field experiment, but the documented setup is a supervised student task in separate rooms and at team stations; this form codes lab_rct under the codebook (PDF pp. 1 and 12-14).

The regression table reports coefficients and p-values without SEs, and the paper pools idea-level scores from both tasks without reporting adjustment for repeated outputs within teams. Cluster-aware precision and the bootstrap resampling unit remain unconfirmed (PDF pp. 15 and 18-20).

Exact Cohen's d values and their standardizer are not printed. The text calls paradigm-relatedness and acceptability medium effects, while Figure 5 places both above the plotted large-effect threshold; retain the graph/text discrepancy rather than deriving numbers (PDF p. 20, printed p. 18).
notes: Screened 2026-10-09. Read the entire markdown conversion, including Appendix 1, references, acknowledgements and the AI-use declaration. All locators use one-based PDF page numbers, followed where useful by the printed page number. Checked source, design, sample, measurement and result pages with PyMuPDF text extraction and inspected Figures 3-5 and Appendix 1 visually in memory. The two tasks share the same randomized sample and are one study; the second project phase is expert evaluation, not a second experiment (PDF p. 12). The tool-development usability work with fifteen participants across three studies is only briefly mentioned, without separately reported creativity outcomes, and is not added to the main sample or coded as additional analyzed studies (PDF p. 13, section 4.1). The 70-person entry is the paper's reported study sample, not a separately stated post-exclusion total; no assignment-stage count or per-arm count is inferred. Country is not explicitly stated; the University of Regensburg recruitment site is retained in who. All ten quality dimensions combine outputs from both tasks. Outcome S1-O11 keeps the four indicators of innovation category together as one categorical measure. No across_people outcome is coded: H4 defines diversity through originality, paradigm relevance and feasibility, and the conclusion repeats that claim without an actual between-person or between-team similarity/diversity statistic (PDF p. 11, Table 1; PDF p. 21, printed p. 19, Results). No after_ai outcome is reported. Task completion time is a process measure and satisfaction is self-report, so neither is counted as a scored-output creativity outcome (PDF p. 17 and PDF p. 21). The higher output-per-unit-time claim is not treated as a separate fluency measure because the paper reports fixed task solutions and no separate fluency score (PDF pp. 12, 14 and 21). No preregistration or explicitly designated primary outcome is reported; aggregate quality is listed first by codebook preference. Means are transcribed from Results prose; SDs, per-arm n, SEs and CIs are not supplied. The statistics_available list does not claim arm_means_sds_ns or regression_coefficient_se. Standardized effects are available only in Figure 5; no exact effect sizes are digitized or calculated. Table 3 labels its coefficient column t-test; the next page expressly interprets these as regression coefficients, which is the labeling used in reported (PDF pp. 18-19). The negative Table 2 t-statistics are retained exactly as printed; treatment_higher reflects the higher AI-arm means. The Results prose broadly describes all means as significantly higher, but Applicability is non-significant in Tables 2 and 3; the form follows those tables (PDF pp. 16-18). No reuse of another paper's participants, data URL, code URL or external statistical supplement is stated in this PDF; unverified search-record leads were not used as evidence.
